extracted.intended_audience: poets, aspiring writers, and patrons/readers of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: A set of poetical reflections and practical maxims (from Horace) about what makes good poetry, how poets should behave toward patrons and audiences, and how works should be presented and judged. Useful as prescriptive/critical guidance for creative writers and poets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and daring
rubrics_metrics.description: The man who trusts himself, and dares step out, Soon sets the fashion to the inferior rout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust your own voice and be prepared to introduce new forms or approaches; boldness and innovation set trends (Horace cites introducing iambics to Italy as an example). Do not merely imitate older models without adding distinctiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional power / ability to move the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: That man I hold true master of his art Who with fictitious woes can wring my heart, Can rouse me, soothe me, pierce me with the thrill Of vain alarm...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A primary test of good poetry is its capacity to move, transport, and affect readers. Technical cleverness is insufficient unless it produces genuine emotional response and imaginative transport (e.g., bearing the reader to Thebes or Athens).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical skill and craftsmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: None but skilled workmen handle workmen's tools: But verses all men scribble, wise or fools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry requires craft and training; mastery of meter, diction, and form distinguishes enduring work from careless scribbling. Invest in learning the technical tools of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pandering to spectacle or the mob
rubrics_metrics.description: I stoop not, I, to catch the rabble's votes By cheap refreshments or by cast-off coats... 'Tis for such the rabble cares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not sacrifice substance for applause, cheap tricks, or visual spectacle. Beware of writing primarily to please a crowd's appetite for display—such tactics can drown the poet's voice and cheapen the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy demands precision and leaves little allowance for flaws
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Tis thought that comedy, because its source Is common life, must be a thing of course, Whereas there's nought so difficult, because There's nowhere less allowance made for flaws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because comedy draws on everyday detail, it tolerates fewer lapses in craft; plot, timing, and economy of detail must be tight. Farce that masks flaws is different from well-crafted comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate age/survival with inherent merit
rubrics_metrics.description: I chafe to hear a poem called third-rate Not as ill written, but as written late; ... To hear your critics for their ancients claim Not charity, but honour and high fame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the critical habit of valuing works merely because they are old or canonized. Judge works on quality rather than age or merely having 'stood the test' of time; surviving reputation can reflect many biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's civic and moral utility
rubrics_metrics.description: He tells of worthy precedents, displays The example of the past to after days, Consoles affliction, and disease allays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should serve social and moral functions: instructing, consoling, preserving ritual and civic memory. Consider how your work contributes to the moral and cultural life of readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt established forms but transform their content
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Archilochus in rhythm and stave, But not the words that dug Lycambes' grave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrow meters, rhythms, or formal devices from predecessors when useful, but reinterpret them with fresh content and perspective; do not be a mere imitator of words or themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from approval and prizes
rubrics_metrics.description: I forswear the drama, if to win Or lose the prize can make me plump or thin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let the pursuit of prizes, patronage, or immediate acclaim dictate artistic choices. Maintain a degree of artistic independence so that external reward does not become the measure of worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage publication expectations and accept loss of control
rubrics_metrics.description: To street and market-place I see you look ... When once sent out, you won't come back, you know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once a work is released it will be handled, judged, and possibly abused by readers and the market; anticipate misreadings, physical wear, and uses you cannot control (e.g., books ending up as school primers). Be deliberate about publication and modest in expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tact, discretion, and modesty in patronage and social dealings
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid all prying; what you're told, keep back, Though wine or anger put you on the rack; ... Look round and round the man you recommend, For yours will be the shame should he offend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate tact and discretion in professional and patron relationships: be modest in self-presentation, keep confidences, choose protégés carefully, and avoid indiscreet talk that can harm reputations and opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambition and proactive effort
rubrics_metrics.description: One man sits still, not hoping to succeed; One makes the journey; he's a man indeed!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success often requires initiative and effort—seek opportunities, patrons, and experiences rather than expecting success to come passively. Virtue and achievement often demand enterprise and risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation, contentment, and practical stability for the writer
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the few years that Fate may grant me still Be all my own, not held at others' will! Let me have books, and stores for one year hence, Nor make my life one flutter of suspense!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sustainable creative life benefits from moderation and some material stability: cultivate contentment and sufficient means to preserve independence and the time to write.
